briefing:
The headline Airfare Price Index (APIx) rose to 103.66 on September 10, 2026, representing an overall market price increase of 3.66% relative to base day medians. upward price adjustments were observed across all three monitored domestic trunk corridors, indicating broader price hardening across key domestic passenger routes. The aggregated upward drift suggests a tightening of carrier yields, driven primarily by extended booking window price adjustments alongside elevated spot fares on high-demand city pairs.

Route-level analysis reveals that the index movement was predominantly anchored by the Calcutta – Bombay corridor, which surged by 6.31% to an APIx of 106.31. This expansion was heavily driven by the 45-day advance booking window (T+45), where median prices escalated from ₹12,915 to ₹16,541 (a price relativity of 128.08), and short-notice T+1 spot departures, which rose from ₹9,584 to ₹12,414.50 (relativity of 129.53). The Delhi – Bengaluru route contributed moderately with an APIx of 103.53 (+3.53%), pushed higher by T+45 advance medians rising from ₹10,048 to ₹11,328 (relativity of 112.74). Meanwhile, the heavily weighted Delhi – Bombay route recorded a subdued APIx of 101.77 (+1.77%), supported by minor increases in T+1 spot fares (median ₹6,898; relativity of 105.64) and T+45 advance fares (median ₹7,019; relativity of 105.01).

Granular scrape logs highlight significant structural fare dispersions and localized pricing anomalies across carrier offerings. On the Calcutta – Bombay corridor at the T+45 window (targeting late October 2026 travel), multiple indirect and connecting itineraries registered near upper price bounds of ₹19,990 (e.g., SpiceJet and Air India connecting flights via Delhi), pulling the route median significantly higher. Conversely, the scraped dataset illustrates a widening price gap between primary hubs and secondary regional facilities: departure options out of satellite airports like Jewar (DXN) and Ghaziabad/Hindon (HDO) for Delhi, and arrivals into Navi Mumbai (NMI) for Bombay, consistently generated discounted entry-level fares. For instance, Akasa Air listed a T+7 fare of ₹4,336 from Jewar to Bombay, substantially lower than the non-stop Delhi Terminal median of ₹6,530.

Looking forward, airfares display clear upward trajectory at extended booking horizons (T+45), signaling forward-capacity pricing power by carriers for late October schedules. From a macroeconomic perspective, policy makers at the Reserve Bank of India and MoSPI should monitor these persistent airfare increases for potential pass-through into the transport and communication component of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). If far-horizon fare strength persists into shorter booking windows, service-driven inflation pressures within the domestic aviation sector could harden, warranting continued analytical oversight.
